UN climate chief urges debt-free climate finance for developing nations
item.description:
UN Climate Change Executive Secretary Simon Stiell has called for a fundamental shift in the global climate finance system, urging developed countries, financial institutions and investors to ensure that funding helps developing nations escape mounting debt pressures and build long-term economic resilience.
Speaking at the Seventh Biennial High-Level Ministerial Dialogue on Climate Finance at COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye, on Friday, Stiell warned that many developing countries remain trapped in a cycle of debt, climate disasters and increasingly expensive borrowing, leaving them with fewer resources to protect their people and economies.
“Climate finance must help countries break free,” he said, stressing that meeting international funding targets alone would not necessarily address the actual financial needs of vulnerable nations.
He argued that climate finance must move beyond funding individual projects towards supporting broader economic transformation, strengthening national institutions and creating conditions that attract more investment at lower costs.
Under the new climate finance goals agreed at COP29, developed countries are expected to take the lead in providing $300 billion annually by 2035, while all actors are expected to work together to scale up financing for developing countries from all sources to $1.3 trillion per year by the same year.
Stiell said the Baku-to-Belém Roadmap provides a pathway towards achieving these targets, but stressed that the way climate finance is delivered must change to make the commitments meaningful.
Explaining the financial challenges facing developing countries, Stiell said the growing threat of floods, wildfires, storms and droughts increases borrowing costs even before disasters occur.
When climate shocks strike, government revenues decline while recovery and reconstruction expenses rise, pushing countries further into debt.
This leaves governments with fewer resources to invest in climate adaptation, resilience and low-emission development, reinforcing a cycle of financial vulnerability.
To break this cycle, he called for climate finance that reflects individual countries' economic circumstances and debt sustainability.
He emphasised that funding must be affordable and tailored to national needs rather than delivered through a one-size-fits-all approach.
While private finance, loans and guarantees remain important for meeting global climate goals, he said grants and highly concessional financing would continue to be essential, particularly for least developed countries (LDCs), small island developing states (SIDS) and other vulnerable economies.
He also called for broader international efforts to address debt burdens so that developing countries are not forced to choose between repaying loans and investing in climate resilience.
Stiell identified easier access to climate finance as another major priority, pointing to the complicated administrative requirements and fragmented funding arrangements that developing countries must navigate.
He said countries often face complex procedures to access funding from multiple programmes and institutions, making it difficult to secure resources when they are needed.
“We need procedures simplified,” he said, calling for stronger coordination among financial institutions and reduced administrative burdens.
He also stressed that international climate finance should align with national development priorities rather than requiring countries to reshape their domestic systems to meet external funding requirements.
National treasuries, local governments, development banks and financial institutions already play important roles in financing development, and these institutions should be strengthened rather than bypassed, he said.
Stiell urged international partners to invest in institutional capacity and help developing countries establish effective systems to access, manage and deploy climate finance.
He also underscored the importance of developing and transferring technologies that support climate-resilient and low-emission development.
The UN climate chief further called for stronger cooperation among governments, climate funds, development banks, financial institutions and private investors to turn national climate plans into tangible investments.
He said climate finance, technology transfer and capacity-building must work together around countries' own priorities, ensuring that funding translates into projects that strengthen resilience and improve people's lives.
As an example, he explained that early grant-based support could help countries build institutional capacity and develop investment pipelines, while concessional finance and risk-sharing instruments could subsequently help projects expand.
He said international climate negotiations and cooperation mechanisms could play an important role in bringing different sources of finance together around national development priorities.
Concluding his remarks, Stiell called for a new approach to international climate finance, saying the biennial ministerial dialogues should help translate commitments into more effective delivery.
Established in 2013, the dialogues have contributed to discussions on global climate finance. However, he said they must now help advance a system that supports long-term development rather than focusing solely on individual funding targets.
“Where every dollar invested in development builds a better future. For all countries,” he said.
His remarks at COP31 highlight a central challenge for developing countries such as Bangladesh: securing not only greater volumes of climate finance but also affordable, accessible and predictable funding that can strengthen economic resilience without deepening existing debt pressures.
This story was produced as part of the COP31 Climate Change Media Partnership, a journalism fellowship organised by Internews' Earth Journalism Network, Informed Earth and the Stanley Center for Peace and Security.

item.title: Shahjalal Airport's third terminal to partially open on 16 December
item.description:
The government plans to partially open the third terminal of Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport in Dhaka on 16 December. Initially, the terminal will begin operations with four flights.

Civil Aviation and Tourism Minister M Rashiduzzaman Millat announced this at a meeting on preparations for the inauguration and operation of the third terminal at the conference room of the Civil Aviation Authority of Bangladesh (CAAB) on Saturday morning.

At the meeting, the minister said opening the third terminal was an important commitment of the current government.

The prime minister’s directives must be given the highest priority to ensure that operations begin on schedule. All relevant agencies must complete their respective tasks within the stipulated timeframe.

The meeting discussed various issues, including the activation of the required immigration booths before the terminal opens, installation of baggage belts and scanners, trial operations and signing of agreements.

Representatives of the relevant agencies exchanged views on progress and identified the steps needed to complete the remaining work.

M Rashiduzzaman Millat said the collective efforts of all concerned over a long period had brought the third terminal to the stage where it was ready to begin operations.

He urged the relevant agencies to implement the decisions taken at the meeting on time.

Among those present were Invest Bangladesh Chairman Chowdhury Ashik Mahmud Bin Harun, Dhaka-18 MP SM Jahangir Hossain, Prime Minister’s Special Assistant Gias Uddin, Civil Aviation and Tourism Ministry Secretary Nurunnahar Chowdhury, and National Board of Revenue Chairman Ahsan Habib.

Law minister: Legal process complete for Hasina’s return, India to decide
item.description:
The government has completed all necessary legal procedures to bring back former prime minister Sheikh Hasina, who was sentenced to death in a crimes against humanity case related to the 2024 uprising.
Her return now depends on a decision by the Indian government, Law Minister Md Asaduzzaman has said.
He made the remarks while responding to questions from journalists at the Bangladesh-China Friendship Conference Centre in Dhaka on Saturday.
Asked about Hasina's possible return and the legal steps involved, the minister said Bangladesh had completed the required procedures and the matter was now in India's hands.
On whether Hasina would have an opportunity to appeal, Asaduzzaman said she would not be entitled to do so under the law enacted by Sheikh Mujibur Rahman.
The minister also said the investigation agency and prosecution would soon begin investigations into crimes against humanity in different districts, adding that the government would provide all necessary support.
Regarding the investigation into bringing the Awami League to trial as a political party, he said the government would not interfere in the process.
The investigation agency and prosecution would be allowed to carry out their duties independently, he added.

item.title: Zelensky: US proposes Ukraine cede territory in exchange for joining Nato
item.description:
The United States suggested for the first time that Ukraine cede land to Russia in exchange for joining Nato, President Volodymyr Zelensky said in comments released Saturday, adding that Russia had rejected an energy target ceasefire at talks this week.
Zelensky said Russia was “betting everything” on this winter’s campaign in its war with Ukraine, while warning that the Kremlin’s demands to redraw Europe’s security architecture are “dangerous” and could lead to more wars.
Zelensky spoke to the media Friday after visits to Denmark and Ireland, where he met with European leaders following two days of US-brokered Ukraine-Russia talks in Abu Dhabi.
The talks ended with no breakthrough in Europe’s worst war since World War II, but all sides agreed that European officials should be included in future negotiations.
“The Americans raised a question: ‘What if Ukraine joins Nato? Would Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?’ This was the first time this had been raised,” Zelensky said in the comments kept under embargo until Saturday.
He said Ukraine was discussing “specific security guarantees from Nato and the EU” and that if Western countries confirmed them “then I will ask our Ukrainian society what it thinks: do we accept it or not? I have no right to make that decision on my own.”
US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff attended the Abu Dhabi talks and then met after with Putin and Zelensky separately.
Moscow turned down a proposal for a ceasefire in attacks on energy targets at the Abu Dhabi talks, Zelensky said.
“On the proposal for an energy ceasefire: the Russians don’t want it,” Zelensky said.
Putin’s proposal for a “humanitarian mission” to Kostyantynivka, Zelensky said, was a ploy to get Kyiv to withdraw from the embattled city and open the road to more settlements in the Donetsk region.
Russia said this year that it had seized the town but Ukraine has said fighting is ongoing.
“Putin simply wants us to leave Kostiantynivka so that they can move in and occupy the entire city that way,” Zelensky said.
Moscow’s troops have inched westwards since launching the invasion in February 2022, but have been unable to seize the whole of the Donetsk region.
Zelensky said the EU and Nato are Europe’s “only real security” and that Moscow’s bid to review the continent’s security was “dangerous because... it is precisely things like this that lead to wars or escalations.”

item.title: Ex-Bangladesh PM Hasina to return home despite 'threat of death'
item.description:
Ousted Bangladesh prime minister Sheikh Hasina, sentenced to capital punishment after she was toppled in 2024, told AFP on Monday she would return home in December despite “the threat of death”.

Hasina fled to India in August 2024 after a student-led uprising ended her iron-fisted 15-year rule, and has remained in hiding ever since.

She was sentenced to death in absentia last year after a Bangladeshi court convicted her of crimes against humanity over a deadly crackdown on protesters.

“I am fully aware of the risks I face if I return,” she told AFP in an email interview.

“But I have made my decision, and no threat of death will keep me away from my own country.”

Her insistence on going back comes days after Bangladesh said she would face execution if she returned, adding that she has no further legal recourse after missing the deadline to appeal against her conviction.

The 79-year-old has repeatedly rejected the legitimacy of the trial.

Dhaka has sought her extradition from India, which says the request is under legal review.

Hasina said the stance was “contradictory”.

“For months, they have demanded my return. Yet now that I am taking practical steps to come home, they appear to be more interested in threatening me… than actually allowing it to happen,” she said.

“Frankly, I find these contradictory statements from the Bangladeshi authorities rather revealing.”

‘If death is the price’

Analysts suggest her promise to return is an attempt to remain politically relevant, retain the loyalty of supporters and keep alive a party that once dominated Bangladesh but whose activities are now banned.

She may also be counting on the possibility that the government would find it difficult to execute the daughter of Bangladesh’s founding leader, despite her death sentence.

Hasina denied that her Awami League party was involved in a recent spate of petrol bomb attacks in Bangladesh, as authorities have alleged.

She said she had no intention of seeking India’s assistance to arrange her return.

“Why would I ask another country to extradite me, when I have already decided to return voluntarily?” she said.

“Extradition is a matter between two sovereign states. India will make its own decisions according to its laws, policies and national interests,” she said.

Hasina also faces a string of other charges, including corruption allegations.

“More than 600 false cases have been filed against me,” she said.

Her lawyers had applied for a Bangladeshi passport and national identity card through the country’s high commission in New Delhi, she said.

“I am already making preparations to return to Bangladesh in December,” she said.

“I do not wish to die. I want to live and continue serving my country. But if death is the price I must pay for returning home, I am prepared to face it. “

item.title: How identity politics is redrawing the India-Bangladesh borderlands
item.description:
THE India–Bangladesh borderlands are not simply spaces of territorial contestation. They are landscapes shaped by shared histories, cultural continuities and deeply intertwined human relationships. These borderlands hold a profound place in Bangladesh’s history.

At Baidyanathtala (later renamed Mujibnagar), near the Indian border, the country’s first government took its oath on April 17, 1971. For decades, despite political tensions and an increasingly securitised border, communities on both sides maintained relationships through cross-border marriages, religious practices, trade, shared languages and everyday interactions.

The political meaning of these borderlands extends beyond territorial security and migration management, raising a more fundamental question: who has the legitimate right to belong?

Recent developments in India’s northeastern border states point towards an increasingly troubling politics of identity. Demolition drives in Assam’s Dhubri district targeting villages largely inhabited by Bengali-speaking Assamese Muslims, the normalisation of derogatory expressions such as Miya, and controversies surrounding villagers’ encounters with the Indian Border Security Force in Tripura have raised questions that extend beyond individual incidents. Who is considered an Indian? Why are certain communities repeatedly required to prove their legitimacy?

These questions reveal a changing relationship between territory, identity and citizenship. For people living along the border, belonging is increasingly negotiated through markers that extend beyond legal documentation: their names, language, attire, religious practices and perceived cultural affiliations.

The border, in this sense, is becoming more than a geographical boundary. It is also a political instrument for distinguishing between those who are considered insiders and those who are treated as outsiders.

This is the cartography of othering: the process through which political narratives redraw the social boundaries of belonging, even within internationally recognised national territories.

The problem becomes particularly acute when religious identity is conflated with national allegiance. Bengali-speaking Muslims in West Bengal, Assam and Tripura are frequently situated within political narratives of illegal migration and demographic insecurity.

Migration and citizenship are legitimate matters of public policy. States have the authority to regulate their borders and establish legal procedures. But when an entire community is persistently viewed through the lens of suspicion, the distinction between immigration enforcement and identity-based exclusion becomes increasingly difficult to maintain.

The political influence of the Bharatiya Janata Party in India’s border states has also contributed to a changing political vocabulary around migration, nationalism and religious identity. Polarising and hateful statements by political leaders, particularly those associated with the political leadership of Assam and West Bengal, have contributed to the normalisation of exclusionary narratives, gradually shifting the boundaries of what is considered acceptable in public discourse.

The territorial imagination underlying some political statements is eq­­u­­ally significant. References by Ind­­ian politicians to Chittagong, Noak­hali and Sylhet as territories that should have belonged to India, or as historical mistakes associated with Partition, are not simply rhetorical provocations. They invoke an unfinished geographical imagination in which historical grievance, religious majoritarianism and territorial nati­o­­n­­alism intersect.

Such narratives deserve scrutiny not because every political statement signals an immediate territorial ambition, but beca­use they can reshape how neighbouring societies perceive one another. The consequences of this politics do not stop at the border fence.

For Bangladesh, these developments carry both political and social implications. Social media has become an important arena where statements and incidents from India’s border states are circulated, interpreted and sometimes amplified without sufficient context.

Reports of discrimination or violence can generate legitimate concern, but misinformation and emotionally charged responses can also deepen antagonism within Bangladesh. The result is a transnational politics of suspicion in which developments on one side of the border influence perceptions and political narratives on the other.

In this context, Myanmar’s Rohin­gya crisis offers a crucial warning. The progressive exclusion of the Roh­i­­n­­gya from citizenship, their institutionalised marginalisation and eventual mass displacement demonstrate how the gradual denial of belonging can develop into a profound humanitarian catastrophe. Bangladesh continues to bear the consequences nea­rly a decade after the mass exodus of 2017.

India and Myanmar are fundamentally different political contexts. The comparison, therefore, should not suggest an inevitable repetition of the Rohingya experience.

History, however, offers an important lesson: major crises rarely emerge overnight. They can begin with the normalisation of suspicion, the politicisation of identity and the gradual erosion of a community’s social and legal legitimacy.

Published in Dawn, November 16th, 2026

Climate adaptation funding shortfall puts Bangladesh under pressure
item.description:
Even after 17 years of Cyclone Aila, the homestead of Md Zia Gain and his wife, Shamima Begum, in Mothbari village of Koyra upazila, Khulna, remains submerged beneath the waters of the Shakbaria River.

A nearly three-kilometre-long and 250-metre-wide channel, formed by tidal currents after an embankment collapsed, has swallowed their home. They now live on the slope of the embankment of the river.

The house of Minoti Sana, a woman in her 60's from the same village, also once stood in what is now the middle of the river. Her land has remained unrecovered since Cyclone Aila.

Ismail Gazi, Yunus Ali and Ilias Gazi, along with many other villagers, share similar stories. They lost their homesteads and have been living on the slopes of embankments for the past 17 years.

Natural disasters are nothing new in Bangladesh. However, the loss of homes, rising salinity and shortages of safe drinking water in coastal areas continue to transform people's lives over the long term. How to address these challenges is being discussed at the COP31 climate conference in Türkiye.

The United Nations Environment Programme's (UNEP) Adaptation Gap Report 2026, published ahead of the conference, highlights the shortfall in climate adaptation finance.

How much funding is needed for adaptation?

According to Bangladesh's third Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC 3.0), the country needs US$8.5 billion annually to implement its adaptation priorities. The same document estimates that the average annual flow of funding for adaptation in the country stands at around US$4 billion.

This leaves an annual shortfall of US$4.5 billion, equivalent to approximately Tk 561.38 billion (Tk 56,138 crore), at an exchange rate of Tk 124.75 per US dollar.

NDC 3.0 states that Bangladesh's annual adaptation financing requirements could rise to between US$12 billion and US$14 billion by 2035.

At the same exchange rate, this would amount to approximately Tk 1,497 billion to Tk 1,746.5 billion (Tk 149,700 crore to Tk 174,650 crore).

Growing needs, insufficient funding

Bangladesh's National Adaptation Plan (NAP) estimates that the country will need a total of US$230 billion to implement 113 initiatives between 2023 and 2050. This amounts to an average of approximately US$8.5 billion annually over 27 years.

The initiatives cover various sectors, including water, agriculture, fisheries and livestock, urban development, disaster management, biodiversity and institutional capacity-building.

UNEP's report draws its estimate of Bangladesh's annual adaptation financing needs of US$12–14 billion by 2035 from the country's third NDC.

The report also states that international public adaptation finance from developed countries to developing nations stood at US$28.7 billion in 2024, an increase of just US$1 billion from the previous year.

The annual adaptation financing needs of developing countries could reach approximately US$305 billion by 2035. This estimate uses 2024 prices and excludes the requirements of the private sector. Including private-sector needs could almost double the total requirement.

At COP30, countries called for adaptation finance to increase at least threefold by 2035. According to UNEP's estimates, even if this target is achieved, it would meet only 20 to 29 per cent of the potential adaptation financing needs of developing countries.

The nature of the financing also matters. In 2024, loans accounted for 55 per cent of international public adaptation finance for developing countries, while grants made up 44 per cent. Nearly half of the loans came on market-based or non-concessional terms.

Experts say Bangladesh needs more grants and low-interest, long-term financing to meet its adaptation costs without placing further pressure on public debt.

Climate finance expert Haseeb Muhammad Irfanullah told Prothom Alo, "Reports published ahead of the COP conferences help us understand changes in the nature and flow of adaptation finance and provide useful insights for negotiations. However, a significant funding gap remains in the flow of finance from developed to developing countries."

Bangladesh still bears the cost of climate damage

According to UNEP's report, Bangladesh allocated at least US$400 million from its revenue budget to the Bangladesh Climate Change Trust Fund between 2010 and the 2017–18 fiscal year. During this period, the authorities approved 512 projects across 18 ministries.

At least 45 per cent of the fund, or more than US$180 million, went towards adaptation activities. However, this amount remains inadequate compared with the country's potential annual requirement of US$12–14 billion.

The Climate Budget Report for the 2026–27 fiscal year estimates climate-related expenditure of Tk 517.46 billion (Tk 51,746 crore) across 25 ministries and divisions. Of this amount, Tk 389.06 billion (Tk 38,906 crore) is allocated to adaptation.

The national budget also proposes an allocation of Tk 1 billion (Tk 100 crore) for the Bangladesh Climate Change Trust Fund.

However, the overall figure for climate-related expenditure does not represent a separate allocation for new adaptation projects. Rather, it reflects climate-related spending identified within the budgets of various ministries and divisions.

Adaptation can reduce climate risks, but it cannot prevent all losses and damage. In the first funding round of the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage, 119 developing countries applied for US$2.8 billion.

However, the fund initially had only US$342 million, equivalent to around one-eighth of the total demand. Complex application procedures and limited institutional capacity also pose barriers to accessing support.

Farah Anjum, Bangladesh country lead at the Global Strategic Communications Council, who is attending COP31, told Prothom Alo, "Although Bangladesh faces significant climate risks, its contribution to global emissions is low. Yet the country has to bear much of the substantial cost of adaptation from its own resources. Developed countries should go beyond their existing commitments and provide accessible grant-based financing, technology transfer and technical assistance. They must also ensure that allocated funds reach vulnerable communities and effectively reduce climate-related losses and damage."

More than half of Bangladesh’s births are now C-sections
item.description:
More than half of the babies born in Bangladesh now arrive through caesarean section.
But how many of those operations are truly necessary?
According to the Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS) 2025, conducted by the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics (BBS) and UNICEF, 51.8% of deliveries in the country now take place through the caesarean method, nearly three times the rate of 12 years ago. The World Health Organization (WHO) says caesarean sections should not be performed without medical necessity, and that a rate of 10% to 15% at the population level is the most appropriate.
The question has become a point of sharp disagreement. Health and Family Welfare Minister Sardar Md Sakhawat Husain says the trend of unnecessary operations has increased at an alarming rate, and alleges that some private clinics and broker networks frighten families into them.
Doctors say they try for normal delivery, that a caesarean is sometimes medically essential, and that some mothers themselves ask for one.
Experts say each pregnancy must be judged on its own circumstances, and that ensuring hospitals are accountable is now a major challenge.
Two days before the last Eid-ul-Azha, at around 7:45am, Fahmid Ahmed (pseudonym) was admitted to a private hospital in the capital with his pregnant wife. Throughout the pregnancy they had been under the care of a doctor at that hospital. Both the mother and the unborn child were in good physical condition, and the couple were mentally prepared for childbirth through the normal process.
Immediately after admission, they were asked, “Have you come for an operation?” The couple were surprised and said they had come for a normal delivery.
A new experience then began. Every now and then, the hospital’s assistant doctors would come to the pregnant mother and say, “Normal delivery is very painful”, “It is very difficult”, and “There will be a lot of complications”. At one point her husband protested: “Why are you saying such things? Where you should be giving encouragement, you are doing the opposite by frightening her.”
As the necessary medical tests continued, the assistant doctors said the unborn child had moved towards the upper part of the abdomen and would have to be delivered through an operation.
The couple still did not give up hope. They contacted the doctor who had treated them throughout the pregnancy and discussed the matter, but that brought no solution. Finally, at around 10:30pm, the woman gave birth through an operation.
From the beginning, the doctor had said he would make every possible effort for a normal delivery. The couple’s experience was different.
Their experience is one part of the overall picture of childbirth among women in the country. Every day, many women like her have to give birth through operations.
The caesarean rate in the country was 19.1% in 2012-13. In 2019, it increased to 36%. In 2025, it reached 51.8%.
The rate varies according to urban and rural areas and economic status. It is 56% in urban areas and 50% in rural areas. Among women from the wealthiest families, 68% give birth through caesarean sections. The rate is 57% in the fourth wealthiest group, 52% in the middle group and 34% among the poorest families.
According to the WHO, caesarean sections should not be performed without medical necessity. Although caesarean rates are increasing worldwide, this has not increased health benefits; rather, the risks for mothers and children have increased. The organisation says a caesarean rate of 10% to 15% at the population level is the most appropriate.
Dr Kishwar Sultana, professor of the Department of Gynaecology and Obstetrics at Holy Family Red Crescent Medical College and Hospital, told Dhaka Tribune there are multiple reasons behind the increase.
First, she said, it needs to be examined whether the rate is increasing more in the private or public sector. Some private-sector hospitals are still not being brought fully under monitoring, and some centres are operated for commercial purposes. However, this cannot be said about all institutions. In some cases, there may be a lack of proper supervision.
Another reason is that mothers who previously had a caesarean section also have to undergo caesarean sections for subsequent childbirths. Some mothers also think that they will have two children, so there is no need to go through the pain of normal delivery. This is called maternal choice.
Pointing out that some matters on the doctors’ side also need to be considered, she said the safety of mother and child is important to doctors. There is no guarantee that both will be fine simply because a normal delivery takes place, and the lengthy process of normal delivery also needs to be considered. Even then, doctors try for normal delivery, but many times patients’ families do not want to accept this. Whenever any problem occurs, the blame is placed on the doctor. No doctor wants anything bad to happen to their patient. However, there is no scope to deny that medical negligence has occurred in some cases, but it is also not right to hold all doctors responsible.
She said repeat caesarean sections are also a major reason. If a mother has a caesarean section once, a caesarean is also performed for her subsequent childbirth. Even for the delivery of a third or fourth child, a caesarean has to be performed. If someone has had two caesarean sections before and is pregnant again, it is assumed that she will have to undergo a caesarean for the third time as well. This is how the number is increasing.
Professor Sultana said that if a woman comes to a doctor and wants a normal delivery, it is her right. If everything is fine during pregnancy, she is advised accordingly, and they wait until the scheduled date. If labour pains do not begin even after that, it is possible to wait and observe for another two to four days, or even up to seven days, while the baby’s heartbeat is monitored.
However, caution is needed from the beginning in some pregnancies. If the mother’s blood pressure rises significantly, the condition of the unborn child deteriorates, the baby’s heartbeat becomes abnormal or the baby passes stool inside the womb, delivery has to be performed on an emergency basis. If the mother starts bleeding, quick measures also need to be taken. caesarean sections have to be performed in these cases. Hospitals with maternity services generally have arrangements for emergency caesarean sections 24 hours a day.
Professor Farhana Dewan, former president of the Obstetrical and Gynaecological Society of Bangladesh (OGSB), also told Dhaka Tribune that doctors try for normal delivery. It is not that caesarean sections are performed intentionally, she said, and many times patients also want them. However, there are many reasons why caesarean deliveries are more common than normal deliveries.
She said caesarean sections are sometimes necessary for medical reasons, for example if there has been a previous caesarean section, if the baby’s position is not correct, if the amniotic fluid decreases, if the baby’s movements decrease or if the mother has a tumour in her uterus. In such cases, a caesarean is performed through prior planning, which is called an elective caesarean. Even after labour pains begin, an emergency caesarean may be necessary for various reasons. These are the indications for caesarean sections, or medical reasons. If everything is normal, doctors try for normal delivery.
Decisions are sometimes taken considering the safety of the baby as well, she said. Doctors become concerned if the baby cannot be monitored properly or if there is a risk that the baby’s condition may deteriorate. Sometimes, if a caesarean is performed late, the baby may develop breathing difficulties, and there may even be a risk of death.
In an ideal situation, Professor Dewan said, every hospital should have a neonatal intensive care unit (NICU), making it possible to provide medical support to newborns when necessary. However, the number of NICU facilities in the country is inadequate compared to the number of deliveries. Many people are unable to receive this service because they do not have the financial means, and beds are often unavailable in government hospitals as well.
In some risky situations, she said, the decision to perform a caesarean is made through prior planning. In other cases, an emergency caesarean has to be performed. For example, if a patient starts bleeding, it is an immediate emergency. Such caesarean sections cannot be performed just anywhere; they have to be performed at a multidisciplinary centre where the necessary facilities and various specialist doctors are available.
Another issue being seen more frequently is maternal request, meaning the mother herself wants a caesarean section. She directly says she will not be able to tolerate the pain of normal delivery and therefore wants a caesarean. This is not seen only in Bangladesh; it is also observed in different countries around the world.
Professor Dewan said mothers are kept under observation throughout pregnancy to determine whether they are prepared for normal delivery. Through regular check-ups, as the scheduled delivery date approaches, it is examined whether the mother has diabetes, high blood pressure or any other physical problem and whether the baby’s position is correct. If everything is fine, normal delivery can be attempted. However, if the mother’s age is very high or she has any other physical problem, additional caution needs to be taken when making the decision.
Professor Dewan said that even if the first child is born through a caesarean section, the second can be delivered through normal delivery. It is necessary, however, to know why the first child was not delivered through normal delivery and why a caesarean had to be performed. Doctors ask every patient about this. If there were reasons such as prolonged labour pains or the cervix not opening even after the scheduled date had passed, normal delivery can be attempted for the second child.
If the mother’s pelvis, or the passage through which the baby is born, is small, there is no possibility of normal delivery. Along with hearing the patient’s previous history, doctors try to understand why a caesarean was performed the first time by examining previous medical documents. If there is a recurring reason that will require a caesarean for subsequent childbirth as well, then it has to be performed. But if a caesarean had to be performed for a temporary reason, such as the baby’s heartbeat decreasing, the water breaking or the umbilical cord coming out first, normal delivery can be attempted for the second child.
At a workshop organised by the Bangladesh Midwifery Society (BMS) on July 6, Health and Family Welfare Minister Sardar Md Sakhawat Husain emphasised the importance of reducing the trend of unnecessary caesarean operations. He said delivery rooms must be established compulsorily at all private clinics and hospitals by July 11, otherwise the licences of the concerned institutions would be cancelled.
The minister said the trend had increased at an alarming rate. At present, he said, a section of people in the country has become excessively profit-oriented, with their main goal being to earn money rather than the welfare of people or the interests of the country. This has also had a negative impact on the healthcare sector.
He said that at one time, most children in the country were born through normal delivery, and there was a long tradition of safe childbirth in rural areas with the assistance of experienced traditional birth attendants. Although healthcare has improved now, the trend of unnecessary caesarean sections for commercial purposes has increased.
Initially, after regular medical examinations, in many cases broker networks and some medical centres frighten family members by warning them of various complications. They create fears such as, “If an operation is not performed, the mother or the child will not survive”, and force families to make the decision to undergo a caesarean section. Naturally, families fall into this trap because they do not want to take risks with the lives of the mother and child.
The minister also alleged that some private clinics and broker networks were encouraging pregnant women to undergo caesarean sections by frightening and intimidating them. He said the government would take strict measures to protect the nation from this situation. At the same time, 100,000 new personnel would be recruited in the health sector, of whom 80,000 would be women, most of them midwifery workers.
Overall, medical necessity, maternal choice, repeat caesarean sections, commercial tendencies among hospitals and limitations in healthcare facilities have emerged as factors behind the increase in the caesarean rate. According to experts, decisions must be made by considering the circumstances of each pregnancy. Creating opportunities for normal delivery by avoiding caesarean sections without medical necessity, and ensuring accountability among hospitals in this regard, are now major challenges.

item.title: Govt cuts import duties on dates, oranges and apples ahead of Ramadan
item.description:
The government on Sunday said import duties on imported dates, oranges, and apples would be reduced temporarily, coinciding with the holy month of Ramadan.
According to an official statement, the cabinet, in its 27th meeting with Prime Minister Tarique Rahman in the chair, decided to reduce duty on imported dates to 5% from 25%, while the rate would remain in effect until March 10, 2027.
It said the import tax on oranges (malta) under HS Code 08051010 and apples under HS Code 08081010 was set at 61%, down from the existing 121.78%, while the makeshift arrangement would remain effective from January 24 to February 23.
The statement said the cabinet gave in-principle and final approval to a revenue board (NBR) proposal to revert from the quarterly setup introduced in the 2026-27 budget, asking standard businesses to submit VAT returns within 15 days of the end of each monthly tax period.
The revised provision is expected to be incorporated in the proposed “Value Added Tax and Supplementary Duty (Amendment) Act, 2026” amending an October 2026 ordinance introducing quarterly VAT filing with monthly submissions.
It recalled that the budget for the 2026-27 fiscal year had relaxed the requirement of submitting VAT returns every month, allowing submission within 15 days of the end of every three months in line with the ordinance.
The statement said the change created obstacles for revenue collection at the field level, making it necessary to amend Section 64 of the Value Added Tax and Supplementary Duty Act, 2012.
The amendment is expected to be approved at the current parliament session, subject to Legislative and Parliamentary Affairs Division vetting.

item.description:
Iran will not let UN inspectors visit its damaged nuclear facilities until the Middle East war has ended and the United States meets its conditions, a senior Iranian official said.
The remarks came days after the International Atomic Energy Agency urged Tehran to take steps towards resuming inspections, which have been suspended since last year’s 12-day war with Israel, when the US also struck Iranian nuclear sites.
“We will not grant the IAEA access to the facilities until Iran’s conditions are met and the war has permanently ended,” Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi said in a televised interview late Sunday.
Iranian nuclear facilities were hit again during the Middle East war which broke out on February 28 when US-Israeli strikes killed Iran’s supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.
IAEA inspectors visited Iran’s Bushehr nuclear power plant in September but have not gained access to other bombed sites including Natanz, Fordow and Isfahan.
Gharibabadi said the agency’s request to inspect damaged facilities was “likely aimed at assessing the effectiveness of American weaponry.”
Efforts to end the Middle East war have made little headway. Tehran is demanding that Washington unfreeze Iranian assets and lift sanctions, among other conditions, in exchange for reopening the Strait of Hormuz, the vital energy shipping route it has blockaded during the conflict.
Iranian officials have said talks on Iran’s nuclear program would come at a later stage.
Earlier this month, the US military announced a $20 million reward for information on Iran’s nuclear program, a move Tehran called “repugnant.”

item.title: The Guardian view on the international court of justice: the ruling against Myanmar should be only the start for the Rohingya | Editorial
item.description:
A landmark finding of genocide marked a good day for international law. But both the court and the Rohingya minority now need sustained support

The finding of the world’s highest court that Myanmar committed genocide is a landmark in international law. But at the heart of this case are “real people, real stories and a real group of human beings”, as Dawda Jallow, the Gambian justice minister, stressed in bringing it. This was one test of how the world has responded to the persecution of the mostly Muslim Rohingya minority in Rakhine state. The international community’s response to the majority judgment will be another.

This is the first time that the international court of justice (ICJ) has found a state guilty of genocide. Around 10,000 Rohingya were killed in the 2016-17 campaign by Myanmar’s military, in many cases gunned down as they fled, with another 700,000 escaping to Bangladesh. The judges found that the aim was to destroy “a substantial part” of the Rohingya people, with the murder of infants, widespread sexual violence and razing of villages not accounted for simply by military objectives.

item.title: Life in the Rohingya camps in Bangladesh is becoming more precarious.
Top UN court finds Myanmar committed state-sponsored genocide against Muslim Rohingya
item.description:
The highest United Nations court ruled on Thursday that thousands of killings and widespread sexual violence by Myanmar’s security forces against the Rohingya Muslim minority population in 2017 amounted to state-sponsored genocide.

The decision, seven years after the case was filed by predominantly Muslim Gambia, marked only the fourth time since the Nazi Holocaust that an international court ruled that the legal threshold to prove genocide had been met.

It was the first time the court held a state responsible for genocide.

“The court finds that Myanmar’s security forces killed thousands of Rohingya civilians, perpetrated widespread acts of sexual violence as well as acts of extreme violence against children and attacked fleeing Rohingya,” presiding Judge Yuji Iwasawa said in a reading of the decision.

The panel found “that the Republic of the Union of Myanmar has committed genocide against the Rohingya group in Northern Rakhine State.”

Myanmar’s government did not immediately respond to a request seeking comment.

Decision is expected to influence other genocide cases

Judges found that Myanmar’s military carried out mass executions of men and boys, committed widespread rape and sexual violence against Rohingya women and burned or razed hundreds of villages during so-called clearance operations.

The military actively spread hate speech targeting the Rohingya population, they said. The court’s ruling is final and cannot be appealed.

Genocide has rarely been established in international courts, largely because prosecutors must prove a specific intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnic, racial or religious group.

The decision by the International Court of Justice, or World Court, is expected to have repercussions far beyond Myanmar, including for South Africa’s 2023 case accusing Israel of genocide in Gaza.

The first major decision by the court in more than a decade on the application of the 1948 Genocide Convention will be pored over by legal experts for clues to how the bench assessed state responsibility in the alleged commission of international crimes.

Both Israel and Myanmar deny genocide and say their forces responded legitimately to attacks by armed groups.

In a major legal victory for Gambia, the court found the state responsible for genocide resulting from a military offensive that drove at least 700,000 Muslim Rohingya from Buddhist-majority Myanmar.

A panel of 15 judges said “the only reasonable inference that can explain Myanmar’s actions is an intention to destroy a substantial part of the protected group namely the Rohingya population in Northern Rakhine state,” meeting the legal threshold for genocide.

The court said Myanmar had an obligation to compensate the Rohingya for the violations it had committed, to be determined at a later date.

Myanmar must also allow the “safe and dignified return to their place of residence and the reunification of families for the Rohingya displaced as a result of Myanmar’s wrongful acts,” it said.

International courts previously only recognised genocide during the 1994 Rwanda genocide, the 1995 Srebrenica killings in Bosnia, and atrocities by Cambodia’s Khmer Rouge in the late 1970s.

While rulings by the ICJ, which settles disputes between states and rules on alleged breaches of international treaties, are final, the court has very limited options to enforce them.

It is distinct from the International Criminal Court, which prosecutes individuals for war crimes, crimes against ​humanity and genocide and can impose jail terms.

item.title: Parts of Bangladesh shut down in protests by Hasina's party, ex-leader Yunus's home set ablaze
item.description:
Parts of Bangladesh shut down as police said two ruling party members were killed and the ancestral home of former leader Muhammad Yunus set ablaze in violence ahead of former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina’s return planned for December.

Hasina’s Awami League party called Thursday’s nationwide lockdown in culmination of a week-long campaign of protests and rallies against the government’s rejection of her request for a new passport and identity card that would allow her return.

To deter violence, 97 platoons of the Bangladesh Border Guard have fanned out across seven districts, including Gopalganj and Faridpur, considered to have many Hasina supporters, its spokesperson, Shariful Islam, said.

Police said former interim leader Yunus’ ancestral home in Chattogram, about 300 km southeast of Dhaka, the capital, was set on fire late on Wednesday.

It is likely that flammable substances were thrown into an unused ground-floor room, Mozammel Haque, chief of the area’s Panchlaish police station, told Reuters, but Yunus’ paternal family members, who live on the upper floors, are safe.

Reuters could not immediately reach the Yunus Centre think tank that speaks on his behalf to seek comment.

Yunus and his government, which led Bangladesh after Hasina’s ouster, have faced hostility from her supporters.

More violence

During the last 10 days of protests, police have reported dozens of crude bomb blasts and incidents of vehicles being set afire in at least 28 districts, injuring several police officials and members of the public, media have said.

Tuesday marks a year since Hasina was sentenced to death by a local court that found her guilty of ordering a deadly crackdown on a student-led uprising against her in 2024.

She has lived in exile in neighbouring India after fleeing Dhaka following violent protests demanding her resignation in August 2024.

On Thursday, authorities detained former education minister Nurul Islam Nahid, who faces charges over several killings during the 2024 protests, from his house in Dhaka, police officer Mohammad Khalid Mansur told Reuters.

At least 37 branches and offices of Grameen Bank, set up by Yunus, have been targeted in arson attacks or attempted fires since Nov 10, with 14 more attacked since midnight on Tuesday, the bank said.

On Tuesday, Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed accused Awami League leaders abroad of inciting supporters to destabilise Bangladesh and torch property, adding that those involved in violence would be identified and prosecuted.

Awami League leaders, most of them in hiding, could not be reached for comment.

item.title: Rooppur plant delivers 350MW to national grid in 8.5hrs
item.description:
The first unit of the Rooppur Nuclear Power Plant supplied 350 megawatts of electricity to the national grid during an eight-and-a-half-hour trial run on Tuesday, marking its first power injection into the grid.
The unit operated without any reported problems before being disconnected for further technical tests. It will be run again for several hours, although the date of the next trial has not yet been fixed.
Project Director Kabir Hossain told Dhaka Tribune that the plant had completed the initial run successfully. Power generation would be increased gradually, depending on the results of further tests.
The trial supply began at 3:16pm on Tuesday in the presence of Science and Technology Minister Faqir Mahbub Anam.
During the tests, engineers monitored the performance and stability of the turbine, generator and systems connecting the plant to the national grid.
Project officials said each stage would assess the plant’s systems, turbine and generator performance, and grid integration. If the results are satisfactory, the plant will require approval from the Bangladesh Atomic Energy Regulatory Authority (BAERA) before the next phase of trial operations.
Under an agreement with the Russian contractor, the first unit is expected to undergo a 10-month trial operation before beginning commercial power supply at full capacity.
Following the trial period, the unit will be provisionally handed over by the Russian contractor to the Bangladesh Atomic Energy Commission. The Nuclear Power Plant Company Bangladesh Ltd (NPCBL) will subsequently begin operating the facility through a government gazette notification.

item.description:
Garment workers’ protests demanding a Tk30,000 minimum monthly wage intensified across Dhaka, Gazipur, Savar and Ashulia on Wednesday, triggering fresh clashes with police, highway blockades and factory closures, while nearly 300 people have been arrested in connection with the continuing unrest.
The escalating confrontation, now in its third week, has disrupted production across Bangladesh’s largest export industry, with workers accusing authorities of delaying wage negotiations and police stepping up operations to contain the violence.
In Gazipur, thousands of workers blocked the Dhaka-Mymensingh highway around 9am, bringing traffic to a standstill in Chhaydana, Hariken and surrounding industrial areas.
A vehicle belonging to Gazipur Metropolitan Police was set ablaze during clashes.
Police confirmed the arson, while law enforcement personnel worked to disperse protesters and restore traffic, which normalised after 2pm.
At least 20 factories in Savar and Ashulia remained closed amid the unrest, while several factories in Gazipur also suspended operations.
In Savar’s Ulail area, thousands of workers from Al-Muslim Group and nearby factories blocked the Dhaka-Aricha highway around 2:30pm.
Clashes erupted when police attempted to clear the road. Officers fired tear gas and rubber bullets after protesters allegedly threw bricks, forcing workers to retreat around 4pm.
Similar confrontations occurred in Ashulia’s Narsinghapur area, where police used tear gas to disperse workers attempting to block the Abdullahpur-Baipail road. Several people, including police personnel, were injured.
In the capital, garment workers clashed with police in Pallabi and became involved in confrontations with local BNP activists in Kafrul following allegations that female workers had been harassed.
Police used sound grenades to restore order.
Police said nearly 300 people had been arrested in 24 cases filed with Savar and Ashulia police stations over alleged sabotage during the continuing protests.
Two leaders of the Green Bangla Garments Workers Federation were also arrested in Dhaka on Tuesday night on allegations of inciting unrest.
The unrest intensified after the minimum wage board postponed its third meeting, scheduled for November 16. The meeting has now been rescheduled for November 23.

item.title: Mideast crisis ‘largest threat’ to energy security ever: IEA
item.description:
IRAN-CRISIS/INSURANCE-SHIPPING

The crisis in the Middle East sparked in February by the US and Israeli bombing of Iran has created the “largest threat” to energy security in history, the International Energy Agency (IEA) warned Thursday.

The agency said in its flagship annual World Energy Outlook that consumers were increasingly footing the bill as the world runs out of ways to absorb the impact of the conflict on energy supplies.

The crisis, just like previous energy shocks, would certainly leave “lasting marks”, the agency warned.

Gulf countries have been struggling to export oil since Iran began blockading the Strait of Hormuz and targeting tankers in the area, following US and Israeli strikes that sparked the crisis in February.

Despite attempts by the United States to escort vessels through the channel -- which pre-crisis carried about one-fifth of global oil shipments -- supply lines remain severely disrupted.

“The Strait of Hormuz crisis has created the largest threat to energy security in history, one that dwarfs the scale of the oil shocks of the 1970s,” IEA Executive Director Fatih Birol wrote in his foreword to the report.

He highlighted the efforts countries had taken to protect households, with producing nations bringing more supplies into the market and using alternative routes, and China buying less from international markets.

“Governments have intervened to try and provide some shelter for consumers, but they have nonetheless faced higher prices and, in some cases, shortfalls of supply,” Birol wrote.

The report said elsewhere that “increasingly it is falling to consumers -- and high prices -- to absorb the impact as other buffers are run down”.

Birol had struck a more hopeful tone in July when he wrote that the oil market was still benefiting from “several cushioning factors”.

‘No pathway’ back

 The IEA’s report comes as nations meet for the COP31 climate talks in Turkey, with governments under pressure to tackle climate change after a year of searing heatwaves and wildfires in Europe, and deadly floods in Nepal.

The agency uses three scenarios for its energy outlook: a cautious one takes into account policies that are currently in place, a middle scenario looks at “stated” government policies including measures that have yet to be adopted, and a third considers a world that reaches net zero emissions by 2050.

In its middle scenario, the IEA forecasts that global oil demand will reach a peak around 2030 before a slow decline, while gas demand would increase until around 2035.

For this report, it also adds two other scenarios based on what might happen if the Middle East crisis persists.

“While the energy sector and the global economy have shown considerable resilience, the longer the crisis lasts, the deeper the effects will be,” Birol said in a press release.

“And I don’t see any credible pathway for the energy world to return to the way it was before.”

item.title: An agreement needed before the Ganges Water Treaty expires
item.description:
The Ganges treaty between Bangladesh and India is set to expire in a few days on 12 December. There has been no news of a new agreement or the renewal of the existing one. It is also unclear whether the two countries are willing to agree on an interim arrangement. The situation is concerning, but people downstream still hold hope.

The first Ganges treaty was signed in 1977. Those who are older might remember the intense political situation in the years leading up to it, particularly surrounding the "Farakka" issue. A few years went by without an agreement even at the end of the last century. During that time, water politics were intense, but the branches of the Ganges in Bangladesh started drying up. The potential lack of an agreement this time could be the final nail in the coffin for these narrow rivers.

As I write this, there is not enough time left for a new agreement. The alternatives are to either have a temporary memorandum of understanding based on the main conditions of the old agreement or renew the agreement for two to three years, as permitted by Article 12. Are the two governments in discussions about such an option? Will they take such a step?

If the potential for such an emergency memorandum slips away due to the uncertainty surrounding Bangladesh's Prime Minister Tarique Rahman's visit to India, it would be disastrous for the region's ecology. Any poor agreement would be preferable to having no agreement at all, especially for those downstream.

The Bangladesh government says they want a new agreement. It should certainly include additional elements compared to the 1996 treaty. At the same time, it should also include more than the 1977 agreement. In that case, a comparative discussion of both agreements is needed. The first treaty was for five years. The second was for 30 years, which was an advancement, but a permanent agreement would be better in the future, with opportunities for review from time to time. Both previous agreements aimed to address the five months of the dry season (January-May). A future agreement should cover the entire year, including flood management strategies, which is also crucial for those downstream.

In 1977, there was an "Agreement" on the Ganges, and the subsequent one was a "Treaty". The first one was signed by ministers, and the second by prime ministers. It is evident that as time has passed, the commitment on water issues between the two countries has deepened. However, there was no provision for an "arbitrator" in either agreement. Including such a provision in the future would be beneficial.

Relations with neighbors can rise and fall, but people in the basin cannot be put at risk in critical matters like water. Therefore, if there is a dispute over water rights, there should be an option to call a third party as an arbitrator. It would also be beneficial to include Nepal in any potential agreement, as they are a strong partner in the flow of the Ganges. If an agreement could be reached among the three countries, the sense of trust among people downstream would increase. Both the 1977 and 1996 agreements considered water availability at the "Farakka Point, " which is harmful to Bangladesh.

In the future, the priority should be to keep the entire flow of the Ganges normal and ensure a fair share for Bangladesh based on that flow. If Bangladesh raises such a demand, India might be unhappy because they have built many infrastructures upstream over the past 40 years that are reducing the river's flow. In such a situation, an alternative for Bangladesh could be to approach the United Nations. Before doing so, it is also necessary to sign the UN's 1997 Watercourses Convention. Because Bangladesh has not signed it, India cannot be pressured to sign it either. It is a significant puzzle why Bangladesh has not yet signed a convention that could be in its national interest.

Dhaka desires a "guarantee clause" as an assurance of minimum water availability in any new agreement. It was present in Article 2 of the 1977 agreement and also differently in Articles 10 and 11 of the 1996 agreement. Therefore, there is no issue including it in the future, and it is crucial for downstream interests. However, over the past 30 to 40 years, the flow of water reaching Farakka has significantly decreased. While the concept of a guarantee clause exists in the agreement documents, only "apolitical" experts could propose how to implement it practically in the riverbed. Indian experts, in particular, suggest they need an additional 5,000 cusecs beyond the previous agreement's allocation.

Currently, there is much speculation in Bangladesh about the future of water distribution. The most pessimistic prediction is that there will be little response from India for a new agreement with more favorable terms for those downstream. The somewhat optimistic reverse prediction is that if this December ends without even a memorandum of understanding, it will be harmful to India as well. It is expected that anti-India sentiment will resurface in Bangladesh, which many in New Delhi likely do not want.

Secondly, Farakka has already caused significant and irreparable harm to the neighboring states of Bihar and West Bengal. Continuing to stop water in the future would bring additional damage to these two states.
Yet, the objections rising in Bihar and West Bengal over a new treaty and the renewal of the old one is itself a puzzle. Perhaps BJP's "political calculations" are at play, which Bangladesh should smartly consider. Perhaps these "movements" are part of negotiations with Dhaka.

For the first time in history, the BJP rules simultaneously in Kolkata, Patna, and New Delhi. This is a good time for any new water agreement because a Delhi-Dhaka understanding is now sufficient. However, at the same time, Bangladesh-India relations are at a historical low, which is a bad time for any new treaty. In this contradictory situation, it is also true that New Delhi's Bangladesh-oriented diplomacy over the past one and a half decades is facing a comprehensive reassessment as we approach 2024.

They clearly indicate a desire to rebuild this relationship. They might also consider the Ganges treaty as part of new "understandings and arrangements" under these new circumstances. Therefore, this moment could be turned into an opportunity for Bangladesh. The agreements of 1977 and 1996 were made in November-December, and moving toward potential prospects in the same season in 2026 might be possible.

Although determining water and water rights is entirely a technical matter, any water agreement comes to fruition only with the conscious touch of politicians. If the BJP government wants to view any potential new treaty as part of a larger political package, it could be uncomfortable for Bangladesh. However, what other choice is there but to face that reality?

The only feasible priority for popular politicians could be to blindly prioritize the protection of ecological interests. Although the opposition parties in Bangladesh are currently silent, they will begin to blame the government for failure as soon as the current treaty expires without any alternative agreement. Therefore, an interim arrangement could only be protective for both Dhaka and Delhi.

#Altaf Parvez is a researcher and writer.

*The opinions expressed here are the writer's own.

Bangladesh could achieve 5.7pc annual growth through fiscal reforms: WB
item.description:
Bangladesh could raise its annual economic growth to 5.7 per cent by boosting domestic revenue, rationalising subsidies, making public spending more efficient and reforming energy pricing, according to a latest World Bank report.

The report titled 'Bangladesh Public Finance Review, 2026' also said if fully implemented, reforms could raise revenue from 8 percent of GDP in FY2025 to 14.4 per cent by FY2035, compared with 10 per cent under limited reforms scenario.

Public spending could rise to 18 per cent of GDP, and the fiscal deficit would stay below 5 per cent throughout and fall to 3.6 per cent by FY2035, it added.

The report mentioned these reforms would build foundations for Bangladesh remain on inclusive growth path and create more and better jobs.

The World Bank’s report finds that low revenues, rising recurrent spending, and growing energy sector fiscal pressures are limiting development spending, particularly investments in human development and infrastructure.

The report also recommends more targeted subsidies, which will protect poor and vulnerable households.

Immediate and sequenced reforms to strengthen revenue mobilisation, improve the efficiency and allocation of public spending, address energy sector fiscal risks will create greater fiscal space for investment in infrastructure and human capital and help Bangladesh return to an inclusive growth path.

Fiscal reform must become a central pillar of the country's growth and jobs strategy, and it is essential to the government's goal of a trillion-dollar economy by 2034.

Key findings:

The economy is not generating enough jobs for its young and growing labour force.

Three in five working-age women are outside the labour force, and 84 per cent of workers are in informal jobs.

Slowing job creation reflects chronic government underinvestment in skills, infrastructure, and reliable energy, which have undermined private sector development

Revenue is very low. Taxes were 6.8 per cent of GDP in FY2025. Total revenue was 8 per cent, less than half the level of peer countries.

Public investment has been squeezed. Capital spending fell from 4.9 per cent of GDP in FY2022 to 2.8 per cent in FY2025. Education spending (1.5 per cent of GDP in FY2025) is well below that of peers.

Debt costs are rising. Interest payments rose from 1.5 per cent of GDP in FY2017 to an estimated 2.6 per cent in FY2026. Heavy borrowing from domestic banks is crowding out private credit.

Energy subsidies are a growing fiscal drain. Power and gas subsidies rose from 0.3 per cent of GDP in FY2018 to 1.5 per cent in FY2025. Recent global energy price spikes are expected to push them higher.

Reforms Needed for Enhancing Fiscal Space

Strengthen revenue governance and modernise tax administration. This means separating tax policy from tax administration, integrating digital systems and moving to a single taxpayer ID.

Streamline tax exemptions and reform VAT and trade taxes. Tax expenditures reached 6.9 per cent of GDP in FY2022, almost as much as total tax revenue.

Move to cost-reflective, rules-based energy pricing. Pair pricing reform with a stronger and more independent energy regulator.

Protect poor households while reforming energy pricing.

Targeted transfers, a stronger social registry and the Family Card platform would replace broad subsidies. Poverty headcount is estimated to have risen from 18.7 per cent in 2022 to 22.5 per cent in 2026. The report is clear that reform needs to improve the effectiveness of support, not reduce protection for vulnerable groups.

Invest more and spend better. Fiscal space created by reform could go to health, education, social protection and infrastructure, supported by better planning and budgeting.

item.description:
United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) President and Bangladesh Foreign Minister Dr Khalilur Rahman visited the Rohingya refugee camps in Ukhiya, Cox's Bazar, a day after the International Court of Justice (ICJ) delivered its ruling in the genocide case against Myanmar.
He arrived at Rohingya Camp 4 in Ukhiya around 8:45am on Friday, where refugees welcomed him.
He spoke with the refugees and listened to their accounts of suffering, insecurity and their desire to return to their homeland.
During the visit, Khalilur Rahman said: "I have come to the camp this morning at a special time, on a special day and at a historic moment. Yesterday (Thursday), the International Court of Justice (ICJ) delivered its ruling on the genocide committed against the Rohingya people by Myanmar. This is a historic event in the court's history."
The Rohingyas view the ICJ ruling as an important step towards securing justice, international recognition and their eventual return to Myanmar.
They hope the ruling will increase international pressure on Myanmar and help pave the way for safe, voluntary and dignified repatriation.
Khin Maung, president of the United Council of Rohingya (UCR), said: "The government and people of Bangladesh saved our lives by providing us with shelter. We are grateful for that. But we do not want to remain in refugee camps forever. Our ultimate goal is to return to our homes in Myanmar. For that, citizenship, security, freedom of movement and fundamental rights must be guaranteed."
He expressed hope that Khalilur Rahman, as president of the UNGA would raise the Rohingya's plight and their aspirations for repatriation more forcefully with the international community.

item.title: Seventh uranium shipment arrives at Rooppur power plant
item.description:
The seventh shipment of uranium from Russia has arrived at the Rooppur Nuclear Power Plant project in Ishwardi, Pabna.
The uranium entered the project site in three specialised trucks around 6:30am on Friday, under tight security supervised by the army and coordinated with other law enforcement agencies.
With the latest shipment, a total of seven uranium consignments have arrived at the project site, including one additional fuel shipment for the first unit and six for the second unit.
According to an earlier announcement by Russia's state nuclear corporation Rosatom, 163 uranium assemblies for the second unit are scheduled to arrive in seven cargo aircraft. Another 48 assemblies for refuelling the first unit will be delivered in two additional cargo shipments.
In total, nine shipments of nuclear fuel are expected to arrive in Bangladesh.
Built with Russian technology and cooperation, the Rooppur Nuclear Power Plant has two VVER-1200 reactor units, each with a generation capacity of 1,200MW. Once both units become fully operational, they will supply a combined 2,400MW of electricity to the national grid.
Meanwhile, trial power generation has already begun at the plant's first unit. On November 17, it began supplying 350MW of electricity to the national grid on a trial basis.
The unit was successfully synchronised with the national grid at 3:16pm that day in the presence of Science and Technology Minister Fakir Mahbub Anam. The plant generated a maximum of 375MW during the process.

item.title: Bangladesh up three notches in UN e-govt index
item.description:
Bangladesh has moved up three places to rank 97th among 194 countries in the United Nations E-Government Development Index (EGDI) 2026, entering the double-digit bracket for the first time.

The country was ranked 100th in the previous edition in 2024. It scored 0.6893 this year, its highest ever, and remains in the "High EGDI" group.

Bangladesh also recorded its all-time highest scores in two of the index's components. Its Online Service Index (OSI) score stood at 0.81, while its Telecommunication Infrastructure Index (TII) score was 0.69, according to release of the Ministry of Posts, Telecommunications and Information Technology.

The results come from the 2026 UN E-Government Survey, which put the Republic of Korea at the top of the digital government ranking. The survey is a biennial publication prepared by the UN Department of Economic and Social Affairs (UN DESA).

The EGDI is a composite measure of a country's readiness, capacity and progress in using e-government to deliver public services. It is a weighted average of normalised scores on three dimensions: the Online Service Index, the Telecommunications Infrastructure Index and the Human Capital Index.

The global average EGDI rose 4.6 per cent, from 0.6382 in 2024 to 0.6675 in 2026. Bangladesh's score of 0.6893 is above the 2026 global average.

Of the 194 countries assessed, 151 now fall in the high or very high EGDI groups, up from 138 in 2024.

item.title: 6.7 magnitude earthquake hits central Peru
item.description:
A 6.7-magnitude earthquake struck central Peru on Friday, Peru’s Defense Ministry said, with preliminary reports indicating minor damage and no fatalities.
The earthquake occurred at 7:09pm (0009 GMT Saturday), 30 kilometers northwest of the city of Junin, at a depth of 129 kilometers.
The United States Geological Survey (USGS) also measured the quake to have a magnitude of 6.7, but estimated its depth to be only 108 kilometers.
Peru’s Defense Minister, Rafael Belaunde, reported that after the earthquake “minor damage was reported to homes in different parts of Junin, as well as interruptions of electricity service and restrictions on highway transit.”
Belaunde added that there had been “no harm to people or impacts to their bodies and health.”
AFP journalists in Lima saw hundreds of people evacuating buildings in the Miraflores district during the quake.
The earthquake was also felt in the capital Lima, as well as Ancash, Ica, Ucayali, Cerro de Pasco, Huanuco and Callao.
Peru’s National Emergency Operation Center (COEN) reported the quake was felt with moderate to strong intensity and that “monitoring continues in vulnerable areas.”
Hernando Tavera, the president of the Peruvian Geophysical Institute, told AFP: “The ground shaking was intense. We have no reports of damage at the moment, but there have been landslides and rockfalls on the hillsides.”
Peru is situated on the so-called Pacific Ring of Fire -- an arc of intense seismic activity stretching from Japan through Southeast Asia and across the Pacific basin.
Seismologists say Peru experiences at least 400 earthquakes per year, three-quarters of which are so weak people do not feel them.
A 5.1-magnitude earthquake in the Junin region in July killed six people, injured 32 others and destroyed 52 homes.
